body: With President Donald Trump and Republicans on the defensive over the cost of groceries, gasoline, housing and healthcare, Democrats expected to spend the summer building momentum ahead of the midterm elections.
That’s not happening.
Instead of assembling a midterms juggernaut, persistent
infighting between
different factions of
Democrats
from Maine to Colorado
threatens
to drown out the
party
’s messaging and undermine its potential success in
November
— including its shot at retaking the US Senate.
The crisis is playing out in real time in Maine, where Senate candidate Graham Platner has demanded to have a say in how he is replaced on the ballot following a which he denies.
Platner has not yet stepped aside despite mounting pressure from more than two-thirds of Senate Democrats and others within the party to do so before a July 13 deadline to replace him on the ballot.

Platner’s rise was bolstered by the progressive wing of the party, which had been wowed by the oysterman’s plain-spoken persona in a matchup against incumbent Susan Collins, a Republican. As Maine’s Democratic party struggles to outline a “transparent” process to choose a successor, Platner’s campaign team is mobilizing supporters to ensure that a more moderate candidate isn’t tapped to replace him.
“The Maine thing is a mess,” said Cornell Belcher, a Democratic strategist.
But the battle lines aren’t limited to Maine.
Over the past month,
the strains between the progressive and moderate wings of the Democratic party have only grown after democratic socialist-backed candidates prevailed in a series of primary races.

“There is a strong anti-establishment, reformist, populist mood in the country — I don’t think it is limited to Democrats. I see it among independents,” says David Axelrod, a former top adviser to President Barack Obama. “It’s not just about Trump. It’s about a system that people feel has failed them and a conventional politics that is inadequate to the moment.”

That anti-establishment mood was showcased in the recent Democratic primaries in Colorado, where first-time politician and Democratic Socialists of America candidate Melat Kiros beat longtime incumbent Representative Diana DeGette in a primary upset.

It’s also rearing its head in Michigan, a swing state Trump carried in 2016 and 2024. Representative Haley Stevens, backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, is running for a US Senate seat against former public health official Abdul El-Sayed, who counts on support from New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and other progressives.

On Tuesday, Stevens and El-Sayed faced off in a primary debate in which they argued over America’s relationship with Israel and the future of the Department of Homeland Security — issues that essentially serve as litmus tests among the different Democratic party factions.

The two candidates are vying to ensure the seat now held by retiring Senator Gary Peters stays in Democratic hands. Retaining control of that is essential if the party has any chance to retake the Senate. Republicans, meanwhile, have largely rallied around Representative Mike Rogers, a well-known lawmaker with national security credentials.
In that race and across the country,
Democratic party moderates worry that more
leftist candidates
who win in the primaries
won’t be palatable
to the broader group of voters who take part in the general election. Trump and GOP officials have already started calling those candidates “communists” who threaten America.

“It is healthy for parties to have these debates,” says Matt Bennett, the top official at the centrist think-tank Third Way. “We do worry the DSA is seeking to not just move the party to the left, but it is a faction, like the Tea Party was that fundamentally altered what Republicans are. That is a long-term, potential problem for Democrats.”

With polls showing continuing voter dissatisfaction over Trump’s handling of the economy and the Iran war, the Democrats still have advantages. And despite a year of redistricting and Supreme Court decisions related to voting that have generally favored Republicans, Democrats are still favored to retake the House of Representatives in November.
The Senate, where Democrats need a net gain of four seats, has always been a tougher hill for Democrats to climb. But almost any path to the majority there includes flipping Maine’s Senate seat.

Looming over the state, and the Democratic party as a whole, is the specter of July 2024. That’s when the party leadership and donor class pushed President Joe Biden to drop out of the race following his dismal debate performance, and he controversially tapped Vice President Kamala Harris as his successor without any opportunity for voters to weigh in on the process.
Maine progressives don’t want that same type of coronation to happen again.

“I admire the Maine Democratic Party’s stated objectives of an open, transparent and legitimate process, and I’m glad they are doing due diligence to have a plan, but I question them keeping the plan a secret until Platner leaves,” says Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee.

Belcher, the Democratic strategist, said there’s been too much focus by the left in Maine on finding their “perfect candidate” to counter Trump and his decade-long appeal toward blue collar voters. Harris’ 7-point win in Maine in her 2024 presidential race shows the party needs a candidate “who can simply energize, mobilize and win the moderate middle of the road Harris 2024 majority.”
The Platner campaign did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Rebecca Katz, a political consultant for Fight Agency, the group working closely with Platner.

To be sure, infighting between the party’s progressive and moderate wings has been going on since at least the 2016 presidential primaries, when Hillary Clinton took longer than anyone expected to defeat Vermont Senator and progressive icon Bernie Sanders. The 2020 presidential race was crowded with multiple candidates, and the moderate Biden emerged from the pack as a consensus pick amid the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Now, progressives are once again trying to flex its power by fielding new types of candidates, like Platner.
But the
internal battles
risk
taking
a toll if
the
candidates
who win out in the primaries
turn off
other party
voters,
or independents.

race
